Social-IQ: A Question Answering Benchmark for Artificial Social Intelligence

A CVPR 2019 benchmark that swaps sentiment/emotion labels for 7,500 open-ended questions over 1,250 in-the-wild YouTube clips, exposing a 30-point gap between human (95.08%) and the best 2019 multimodal model (64.82%) at judging social situations.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2019, "social intelligence" in machine learning meant sentiment scores and a handful of emotion categories. CMU-MOSEI, MOSI, and similar corpora reduced every social moment to a numeric label — a valence score, a discrete emotion tag — because that is what was easy to annotate and easy to score. But numeric supervision cannot express why a group seems tense, or how two people are managing a disagreement, or what a raised eyebrow is doing in a conversation. Those require language: open-ended reasoning about intentions, mental states, and the causal structure of an interaction — the kind of probing question-answering already offered for objects (VQA, COCO-QA), for text (bAbI, MCTest), and for narrative video (MovieQA, TVQA). None of those QA benchmarks targeted social reasoning specifically; MovieQA and TVQA test plot and event comprehension in scripted movies and TV shows, and VQA-style datasets ask about what is visible in a single frame, not about intent, attitude, or relationship dynamics between people.

Social-IQ's gap claim is precise: there was no benchmark whose questions are explicitly required to probe social intelligence — judgment of social situations, processing of intelligent human behavior, inference about mental states/traits/attitudes, and grounding via reference to unnamed people ("the woman in the tense voice") — over naturalistic, unscripted video. Movies are scripted and rehearsed; Social-IQ instead scrapes ordinary YouTube footage (talk-show panels, pranks, family arguments) precisely because scripted drama compresses and stylizes social behavior in ways real interactions don't. The paper's stated bet is that unconstrained, free-text QA is what "opens the door to explainable social intelligence" — a model that can answer why is a model whose reasoning can at least in principle be checked, unlike a model that only outputs a valence number.

// how it works

The method

Social-IQ is a construction paper as much as a modeling paper: the contribution is a rigorously-annotated dataset plus a taxonomy that defines, in psychometric terms, what counts as a valid "social intelligence" question. Drawing on decades of psychology and sociology work on measuring social intelligence (Thorndike 1920, Piotr Sztompka's and Max Weber's definitions of a social situation), the authors specify four criteria a question must satisfy at least one of: (1) judgment in social situations — e.g. "Are the people in this group getting along?"; (2) processing human intelligent behavior — how/why people act or react, explicitly excluding pure action-recognition questions like "is the man lifting weights?"; (3) understanding mental state, trait, attitude, and attributes — e.g. "Does the man in the black robe seem like he can manage high stress?"; and (4) memory for referencing and grounding — resolving descriptions like "the woman who was sad when coming into the house" without ever using a name. Every question and every answer is further tagged with one of three complexity levels (easy / intermediate / advanced) via Likert-scale annotator vote.

Getting from that taxonomy to a dataset took a 6-stage annotation pipeline run over 14 months across three annotation seasons by 50 trained CMU undergraduates. Stage 1 harvested 2,000 candidate videos from YouTube using search terms following the precedent set by CMU-MOSEI (250 diverse terms), keeping only videos with a detected face (via MTCNN) in at least 80% of frames. Stage 2 had two annotators independently confirm each video actually contains a genuine social situation — interaction, opinion-sharing, communication — cutting the set to 1,250 videos (1,239 minutes of annotated content drawn from 10,529 minutes of raw footage). Stages 3–4 (question creation and validation) had two annotators write 3 questions each per video with a candidate correct/incorrect answer, then two different annotators validate or reject each question against the four-criteria rubric, cycling rejects back to stage 3. Stages 5–6 (answering and answer validation) had two more, again different, annotators each write 3 correct and 2 incorrect answers per question (blind to prior answers), then a final pair of validators check correctness and diversity. The result: exactly 6 questions per video (7,500 total), 4 correct + 3 incorrect answers per question (30,000 correct + 22,500 incorrect = 52,500 total answers). Annotator quality was policed continuously — 8 dedicated workshops over the year, individual retraining for underperforming annotators, and monetary incentives explicitly tied to creativity rather than throughput.

The design also builds in three anti-bias measures the authors call out directly: annotators are unlikely to have pre-existing familiarity with arbitrary YouTube clips (unlike famous movies in MovieQA/TVQA, which risks contamination from cultural familiarity rather than the video itself); every stage of question/answer creation is separated from validation by a disjoint set of annotators; and answers are required to be explanatory rather than terse — Social-IQ's average answer is nearly double the length of prior multimodal QA datasets.

// what they found

The results

The dataset's own statistics already make an argument. Questions average 10.87 words and answers 10.46 words — versus an average of 1.24 to 5.3 words per answer across prior multimodal QA sets (VQA, MCTest, DAQUAR, TVQA, MovieQA), the direct payoff of requiring explanatory rather than one-word answers. Question types skew toward causal reasoning: why questions make up 34% of the dataset and how questions 26% — together 60% of all questions — compared to prior video/image QA benchmarks where what (object) and who questions dominate. Complexity is skewed hard toward the difficult end: 41% of questions/answers are labeled advanced, 40% intermediate, and only 19% easy. Videos span a broad topical range (politics, sports, entertainment, comedy, activism) and typically feature 1–2 active characters, though a meaningful fraction involve 5 or more.

On the modeling side, the authors ran two families of baselines. The first isolates potential dataset bias: an answer-only model (Q+A, BERT embeddings, no video/audio/transcript) scores 57.02% binary accuracy — 7 points above the 50% random floor, a modest but real above-chance signal purely from linguistic patterns in questions and answers. Adding transcript (Q+A+T) barely moves the needle to 57.87%; adding acoustic features from COVAREP (Q+A+Ac) to 57.22%; but adding visual features from DenseNet161 scene embeddings (Q+A+V) jumps to 63.91%, the single largest lift from any one modality and evidence that answering actually requires looking at the video, not just reading text.

The second family ports seven state-of-the-art architectures wholesale from MovieQA, TVQA, and CMU-MOSEI leaderboards — LMN, FVTA, End-to-End Memory Networks, MDAM, MSM, Tensor Fusion Network (TFN), and Memory Fusion Network (MFN) — plus a new hybrid, Tensor-MFN, built by architecture/hyperparameter search combining TFN and MFN. Tensor-MFN comes out on top at 64.82% binary accuracy (A2) and 34.14% four-way multiple-choice accuracy (A4, chance = 25%). Human performance, measured on the same binary task by annotators who had not seen the question or video beforehand, is 95.08%.

The headline number the paper hangs its conclusion on is the 30.26-point gap between human performance (95.08%) and the best model (Tensor-MFN, 64.82%) on the binary task — evidence, in the authors' framing, that Social-IQ demands a level of social reasoning 2019-era multimodal fusion architectures could not yet deliver.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

Social-IQ's annotation process is unusually careful for its era — disjoint annotator pools per stage, continuous supervision, explicit complexity labeling — and the answer-only bias probe (Q+A alone barely beats random) is exactly the kind of self-skepticism a benchmark paper should run. But read seven years later, several aspects of the evaluation design look dated or under-specified, and they matter for anyone citing Social-IQ today (as SOTOPIA, MMToM-QA, and AgentSense do) as evidence about what static QA benchmarks can and cannot capture about social intelligence.

baselines

Every "state of the art" baseline (LMN, FVTA, MDAM, MSM, TFN, MFN, E2E Memory Networks) is ported wholesale from MovieQA/TVQA/CMU-MOSEI circa 2016–2018 — none was designed for or pretrained on anything resembling social-situation reasoning, and none is a large pretrained multimodal model (this predates CLIP, video-language transformers, and instruction-tuned LLMs entirely). The paper's own new contribution, Tensor-MFN, is a hyperparameter-searched hybrid of two existing fusion methods (TFN + MFN) rather than an architecture purpose-built for the task, so the reported 64.82% ceiling says more about 2018-era multimodal fusion in general than about Social-IQ's specific reasoning demands.

contamination

Not addressed at all — understandably, since the paper predates web-scale LLM pretraining. But this is exactly the liability that later social-benchmark work has to reckon with: the videos are unmodified public YouTube clips, and if their transcripts, comments, or descriptions were later scraped into any model's pretraining corpus, a modern LLM could get partial credit for memorized text rather than social reasoning. No decontamination check exists for this dataset against post-2019 pretraining corpora.

what's missed

Two gaps stand out. First, despite the paper's stated goal of "explainable" social intelligence via open-ended answers, the actual evaluation reduces every question to discriminative accuracy — pick the correct pre-written answer from a fixed pool of 4 — never generation or free-form judgment of an answer's reasoning quality; the explainability payoff is realized only at annotation time, not at eval time. Second, and this is the thread SOTOPIA (2023) pulls on directly: Social-IQ tests passive comprehension of a pre-recorded, already-finished social situation. It never asks a model to act — to generate its own socially appropriate behavior inside a live, unfolding interaction. A model that aces Social-IQ has demonstrated it can judge someone else's social behavior after the fact; that is a meaningfully different (and easier) capability than producing socially competent behavior of one's own, which is exactly the gap SOTOPIA's interactive, agent-vs-agent evaluation was built to fill.

would raise confidence

A modern re-run scoring today's video-language models (with an explicit decontamination pass given the public-YouTube provenance) would tell us whether the 30-point human gap has actually closed or just moved. An adversarial-filtering pass over the incorrect-answer pool (in the style of SWAG/HellaSwag) would help separate genuine social reasoning from residual answer-only artifacts, given the paper's own Q+A-only baseline already clears random by 7 points. And reporting inter-annotator agreement statistics on the "human performance" figure — not just a single 95.08% point estimate from CMU-trained validators — would clarify how much of that ceiling reflects annotators who already internalized the dataset's own construction criteria.

// bottom line

Social-IQ is a genuinely careful piece of dataset construction and a fair historical marker: it is one of the first attempts to operationalize social intelligence as open-ended QA rather than numeric affect labels, and its 30-point human/model gap was a real, useful challenge signal in 2019. But its baselines are frozen at pre-LLM multimodal fusion, its evaluation is discriminative despite an explainability pitch, and — most importantly for how it's cited today — it measures whether a model can correctly judge a finished social scene, not whether a model can behave well inside one. That distinction is precisely what later interactive benchmarks like SOTOPIA were built to address.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Social-IQ (CVPR 2019) reframes "social intelligence" as an open-ended QA task rather than a numeric sentiment/emotion label, built from 1,250 in-the-wild YouTube videos via a 6-stage, 50-annotator, 14-month pipeline into 7,500 questions and 52,500 answers (30,000 correct / 22,500 incorrect).
  2. The dataset is deliberately harder and more causal than prior multimodal QA: 60% of questions start with why/how, 41% are labeled advanced complexity, and answers average 10.46 words versus 1.24–5.3 words in prior VQA-style datasets — while an answer-only baseline barely beats random (57.02% vs. 50%), suggesting the difficulty is largely genuine rather than an artifact.
  3. Even the best 2018-era multimodal fusion model (Tensor-MFN) reached only 64.82% binary accuracy against a 95.08% human ceiling, a 30.26-point gap — but the benchmark only ever tests passive judgment of a finished scene, never a model's own social behavior in a live interaction, which is exactly the limitation SOTOPIA's interactive evaluation, and later benchmarks like MMToM-QA and AgentSense, were built to move past.
